title: A forest officer's view of the tiger
body: Meera is a forest officer posted in a tiger reserve in central India. In a meeting with nearby villagers she explains why the reserve matters. A tiger needs a large territory with enough deer, wild boar and other prey. The prey animals in turn need grasslands, streams and healthy forest. If poachers kill tigers or the forest is cut, the whole chain is disturbed. 'When we protect the tiger,' she says, 'we have to protect the grass, the water and every animal the tiger depends on. So saving the tiger is a way of saving the whole forest.' She also tells them that the trade in tiger skins and bones once pushed tigers close to extinction, which is why special protection was started in 1973.

title: A village committee and a degraded forest
body: Near a village in eastern India, a patch of forest land managed by the forest department had become badly degraded because of heavy grazing and illegal felling. The villagers formed a village forest protection committee. Members took turns guarding the forest, stopped outsiders from cutting trees and helped plant saplings of local species. The forest department worked with the committee and recorded its work. After some years the forest recovered. The villagers were allowed to collect leaves, fruits, fodder and other produce from the forest, and when timber was later harvested from the protected area, the committee received a share of it.
